reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) shows that low friction and high wear resistance occur in inert environments via an ultra-nanocrystalline layer with inverse Hall-Petch behavior, and explicitly states that oxidation is detrimental. The hypothesis, however, proposes that oxygen forms a protective oxide film that reduces wear via the same inverse Hall-Petch mechanism, which directly contradicts the cited finding that inert environments mitigate oxidation to achieve low wear. The key premise that oxygen promotes a beneficial tribo-oxide film is unsupported and misrepresents the cited evidence.
premises: CoCrFeMnNi forms an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer under sliding in inert environments, giving low friction and high wear resistance
This nanocrystalline layer exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior (hardening with grain refinement)
Oxygen-rich environments are detrimental to wear performance in this alloy, and inert environments mitigate oxidation
Tribo-oxidation in oxygen-rich environments will dynamically form a protective ultra-nanocrystalline oxide film
